newsitem.title: MEXICO: Analysts see Hacienda's hand in Mexico peso plan.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Hacienda's hand in Mexico peso plan.

text.p: The hand of the Finance Ministry (Hacienda) is behind a shift this week, in action and in words, towards knocking some of the steam out of the unfaltering Mexican peso, analysts said.

They say a warning from the Exchange Commission on Wednesday was a sign Hacienda concerns over a powerhouse peso have overcome reticence on the part of Banco de Mexico to brake the strength of the free-floating currency.
"The theory is that Hacienda is dragging Banco de Mexico reluctantly," said Banker's Trust economist Denis Parisien.

Hacienda and central bank officials on the Exchange Commission bumped up the amount of the auction of dollar put options to $500 million for August from its previous $300 million. A second auction could also be held.
The program was started in mid-1996 to help build international reserves.

But on Wednesday, the high-level commission added it was concerned the strong peso could harm the sustainability of the economic recovery, adding that an "important" flow of funds could persist over the next few months.
The government has come under heavy pressure from exporters and high-profile business groups to stop the real appreciation of the peso, seen as eventually cutting into the trade surplus.
But the central bank has also been concerned with throttling inflation.
Caught in the middle has been the peso, given a boost by a flood of capital into Mexico's stock market and from high levels of direct foreign investment.
"I think the statement and the increase in the dollar put option was a compromise," Parisien said.

Despite the mixed membership on the commission, Hacienda has the final say, and analysts add that the latest release from the commission bears a striking resemblance to earlier Finance Ministry policy statements.
"My personal impression without being certain is that this was 'pushed' by the Finance Ministry," said one Mexico City economist.
"The Finance Ministry is much more preoccupied that the parity is not too strong than the Banco de Mexico, which does not see anything wrong with a strong peso," he said.
Banco de Mexico deputy governor Francisco Gil Diaz told reporters the central bank will keep using the program.

"We have been obtaining foreign currency (with the option plan) since it came into effect about a year ago, and we will keep using the system," Gil Diaz was quoted on Friday by El Economista as saying.
The auctions to date have had little effect in dampening the peso's strength, which is why the bank may have been willing to cede ground, analysts said.
Santander Investment said in a report that the dollar put option mechanism alone may prove insufficient.
"We anticipate that international capital flows to Mexico will continue, keeping the peso relatively strong for the rest of the year," economists Hector Chavez and Enrique Ramirez said.

Should the central bank really want to shift the underlying strength of the peso, it could change its liquidity objective in the money markets instead of leaving the markets neutral, as it has done recently.
"If Banco de Mexico really wanted to see a cheaper peso, they would obviously change the daily liquidity objective... They would turn on the tap and turn it to positive," Parisien said.
((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728 9559))
